newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Ex-communist Kazakhs to pioneer pension reform.
newsitem.headline: Ex-communist Kazakhs to pioneer pension reform.

text.p: Kazakhstan said on Tuesday it would become the first post-communist state to launch a radical reform of its national pension scheme by arranging a network of private pension funds next year.
"We are the first to follow this road," Grigory Marchenko, Chairman of the National Securities Commission, told a news conference.
On June 20 President Nursultan Nazarbayev promulgated Kazakhstan's new law on the national pension scheme adopted earlier by parliament.
The law envisages the launch of an alternative network of private pension funds starting in January 1998.
"The main thing is to have the political will," Marchenko said. In reforming its pension scheme, Kazakhstan was outstripping such reformist ex-communist states as Poland, Hungary and Slovenia.

Poland plans a reform of its pension scheme, but preparation may be delayed by forthcoming parliamentary elections. Some small private pension funds exist in other ex-communist states such as the Czech republic but the overwhelming burden is borne by the state.
The idea of setting up private pension funds was partly borrowed from Chile, which started reforming its national pension scheme in 1981.
"Chile's experience is very positive," Marchenko said.
He said dozens of private pension funds could appear next year in the resource-rich Central Asian state, which is five times bigger than France and has a population of just 16.7 million.
"These companies, like in Chile, are expected to become with time important institutional investors helping to develop a number of markets inside Kazakhstan," he said.
Under the new law 10 percent of the monthly salary of a Kazakh employee would be put into a pension account.
Marchenko said that special companies would be licensed by the government to manage assets of private pension funds.

He said that to avoid risks these companies would have to invest some 20 percent of the funds' assets in shares of large Kazakh companies traded on the domestic stock market which the government plans to set in motion in September this year.
"These will be reliable companies...they represent oil and gas, mining and banking sectors," Marchenko said.
At least 50 percent of the assets of private funds will be invested in Kazakhstan's state securities market, he said.
But Marchenko said these managing companies were unlikely to rake in super profits.
"Those wishing to earn quickly and easily must not bother," he said, adding that profits were likely to appear only on the third year of the pension reform.
In contrast to Chile, the former Soviet republic is going to have a state-run pension fund for those still lacking confidence in the efficiency of its nascent market economy, Marchenko said.

The current pension fund inherited from Soviet times has gone bankrupt, owing pensioners nearly $500 million, but the government has undertaken to cover all arrears by the year-end, raising money from cash privatisation, international financial markets and cuts in this year's budget.
Marchenko said he expected that up to 60 percent of Kazakh pensioners would prefer to put money in the state fund, being attracted rather by state guarantees than high interest paid.
But he said the future was for private finds.
"All those who worked out the new concept of the national pension scheme will put their money only in private funds."

He said he hoped for a changing mentality in the population within the next four or five years, when money will start pouring out of the state fund into more lucrative private ones. "By 2005, the share of the state fund may shrink to 20 percent of all pension savings," he said.
